8.title: a path
8.hook: a path — eight parts, a life
8.tomorrow: mindfulness before it was a corporate wellness word
8.howItsDone: Buddhists practice the eightfold path as a whole way of life: keeping ethical precepts in speech, action and work, meditating, and studying the teaching; the eight-spoked wheel, the dharmachakra, is one of Buddhism's most common symbols.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the third truth, nirodha, the flame going out. Your line was there is an end. Did you notice something hard actually ending? Day eight.

Think of the last time someone told you what was wrong, and then just left. A mechanic who says your car has a problem and walks off. A friend who says you seem stressed, and changes the subject. It's worse than not knowing. The first three truths could have been like that. There is dukkha. It comes from thirst. It can end. Great. How? The Buddha didn't leave it there. The fourth truth isn't an idea at all. It's directions. And they aren't a one-time fix, like a pill. They're something you walk, every day, for a life.
screen: `THE PROBLEM, THEN SILENCE.` → `GREAT. HOW?` → `THE FOURTH TRUTH IS DIRECTIONS.`

segments.voice: The fourth noble truth is magga, the path. The way that leads to the end of dukkha. It has eight parts, so it's called the noble eightfold path. Here they are, quickly. Right view. Right intention. Right speech. Right action. Right livelihood. Right effort. Right mindfulness. Right concentration. The word translated right is samma, and it's gentler than it sounds in English. It means whole, complete, well-tuned, the way a chord is right. Not right as opposed to wrong answers on a test. Right the way a thing fits. In one of the old discourses, a nun named Dhammadinna sorts the eight into three bundles. Wisdom: seeing clearly and meaning well. Conduct: how you speak, act and earn a living. And meditation: effort, mindfulness, concentration. Notice what that means. Half the path isn't sitting on a cushion. It's how you talk to your sister and how you make your money. And here's the key thing people get wrong. The eight aren't steps you finish one at a time, like levels. They're more like the eight spokes of a wheel, and many Buddhists read the eight-spoked dharma wheel exactly that way. They turn together. A little honesty helps meditation. A little meditation helps honesty. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, says it plainly: "The best of ways is the eightfold; the best of truths the four words." The four words are the four truths you now know. And the eightfold way is how you walk them. Not believe them. Walk them.
screen: `MAGGA — THE PATH.` · `EIGHT PARTS, EACH ONE SAMMA.` · `WISDOM, CONDUCT, MEDITATION.` · `SPOKES OF A WHEEL, NOT STEPS.` · then, large: `THE BEST OF WAYS IS THE EIGHTFOLD.`

segments.voice: Today the bell gives you a little longer: about forty-five seconds. Sit comfortably. Pick just one spoke of the wheel for today. Maybe speech: one thing you'll say more kindly. Maybe action: one small harm you'll skip. Maybe livelihood: one moment at work you'll do honestly. Hold that one spoke in mind, and breathe with it. You don't have to walk all eight today. One step is still walking. The bell holds the time.
The fourth. The fourth noble truth, magga: an eightfold path, wisdom, conduct and meditation, turning together like a wheel. Eighth word.
Your line: walk. Today, take the spoke you picked and actually use it once, in a real conversation or a real choice. Day eight.

screen: `DAY 8 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: MINDFULNESS BEFORE IT WAS A CORPORATE WELLNESS WORD.`

9.title: mindfulness before it was a corporate wellness word
9.hook: mindfulness before it was a corporate wellness word
9.tomorrow: why meditation starts and ends with a sound
9.howItsDone: Buddhists practice sati in sitting meditation, in walking, and in daily tasks, often following the four foundations of mindfulness: the body, feelings, the mind, and mental patterns, as taught in the Satipatthana Sutta.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the fourth truth, the eightfold path, eight spokes turning together. Your line was walk. Which spoke did you use? Day nine.

Mindfulness is everywhere now. It's on coloring books, on water bottles, in the employee handbook between the dental plan and the parking policy. There are mindfulness apps, mindfulness snacks, a mindfulness module you have to finish before Friday. It can start to sound like a vitamin: take ten minutes, be more productive. But the word has a much older life. It's a translation, chosen by a Victorian scholar, for a word the Buddha used all the time. And the original has a surprise folded inside it. It's related to remembering.
screen: `MINDFULNESS: ON A WATER BOTTLE.` → `A VICTORIAN TRANSLATION.` → `AN OLDER WORD UNDERNEATH.`

segments.voice: Sati. It's the seventh spoke of the path you met yesterday: right mindfulness. The word is related to the Sanskrit smriti, memory, remembrance. So sati isn't only paying attention. It's remembering to pay attention. Keeping something in mind, and not letting it slip. Think of a gatekeeper at a city gate, which is an image the old texts actually use. The gatekeeper doesn't fight everyone. He just remembers to stay at the gate and notice who's coming in. When English-speaking scholars first translated the Buddha's discourses in the eighteen-eighties, T. W. Rhys Davids used the word mindfulness for sati. It stuck. More than a century later, teachers in hospitals and clinics took the practice into secular settings, and from there it spread into offices, schools and apps. That's not a bad thing. It's helped a lot of people. But notice what came along and what got left behind. In the texts, sati is one spoke of eight. It sits next to right speech, right action and right livelihood. It's not a tool for doing anything more efficiently. It's part of a whole path meant to end dukkha, and it's meant to notice everything: the breath, the body, the feelings, the mind, even whether what you're doing is kind. The Buddha's great teaching on it lays out four places to set this remembering: body, feelings, mind, and the patterns of experience. Sati doesn't judge. It doesn't fix. It notices, clearly, and it remembers to keep noticing. Which turns out to be the hardest and simplest thing there is.
screen: `SATI — RIGHT MINDFULNESS.` · `RELATED TO SMRITI, MEMORY.` · `THE GATEKEEPER AT THE GATE.` · `ONE SPOKE OF EIGHT.` · then, large: `REMEMBER TO NOTICE.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about forty-five seconds. Be the gatekeeper. Sit, and rest your attention on the breath. When a thought comes in, and it will, don't chase it and don't slam the gate. Just notice: thought. Then remember to come back to the breath. Each time you remember, that's sati. Forgetting isn't failing. Remembering is the practice. The bell holds the time.
Sati. Mindfulness, but older and fuller: remembering to notice, the gatekeeper at the gate. Ninth word.
Your line: notice. Pick one ordinary thing today, washing a cup, climbing stairs, and do it remembering that you're doing it, start to finish. Day nine.

10.title: why meditation starts and ends with a sound
10.hook: why meditation starts and ends with a sound
10.howItsDone: In many Buddhist temples and meditation groups, a bell or gong opens and closes each sitting and marks the monastic day; in Plum Village communities people pause and breathe whenever a bell sounds, and in Japan many temples ring their great bell 108 times on New Year's Eve.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sati, remembering to notice, the gatekeeper at the gate. Your line was notice. What ordinary thing did you do start to finish? Day ten.

Every one of these lessons has started with a sound. You've heard it ten times now. Maybe you've stopped hearing it. In meditation halls around the world, from a monastery in Thailand to a Zen temple in Kyoto to a church basement where a group sits on Tuesday nights, the same thing happens. Someone strikes a bell. Everyone goes quiet. Minutes later, the bell again, and people stretch and blink. Why a bell? Why not a timer, or someone saying okay, start? Today, the sound you've been hearing since day one.
screen: `TEN DAYS, THE SAME SOUND.` → `A BELL, AND EVERYONE GOES QUIET.` → `WHY A BELL?`

segments.voice: Bells are old in Buddhist life. Temples across Asia hang great bronze bells that are struck with a swinging wooden beam, and small bells, bowls and gongs mark the hours of the monastic day: time to wake, time to eat, time to sit. In Japan, on New Year's Eve, many temples ring their great bell a hundred and eight times, one strike for each of the hundred and eight troubles of the heart that Buddhist tradition counts. People line up in the cold to take a turn. But the simplest reason for a bell is the one you already know from ten days here. A bell is a sound that begins, and then fades, and then is gone. You can follow it all the way down to silence. And following it is a tiny meditation all by itself. Your mind has to arrive in the present to hear it at all. You can't listen to a bell yesterday. The Vietnamese Zen teacher Thich Nhat Hanh taught his communities to stop whatever they're doing when a bell sounds, even mid-sentence, and take three breaths. He asked people not to say they hit the bell, but that they invite it to sound. Small change, and it tells you everything: the bell isn't a starting gun. It's a welcome. There's another thing a bell does. It holds the time for you. When the bell will tell you when to stop, you don't need to peek at the clock. You're free to just be here. That's why this app ends every sit with it. The bell keeps the time so you don't have to.
screen: `BELLS MARK THE MONASTIC DAY.` · `A HUNDRED AND EIGHT STRIKES.` · `A SOUND YOU FOLLOW TO SILENCE.` · `INVITE THE BELL, DON'T HIT IT.` · then, large: `THE BELL HOLDS THE TIME.`

segments.voice: When the bell sounds this time, don't just wait for it to be over. Follow it. Listen to the strike, then the ring, then the long fade, all the way down until you can't tell if you're still hearing it. Then stay there, in whatever's left, for the rest of the forty-five seconds. When your mind wanders, you'll hear the next bell to call you back. The bell holds the time.
The bell. A sound that begins and fades, calling the mind into the present, and holding the time so you don't have to. Tenth word.
Your line: arrive. Choose a sound you'll hear today, a phone buzz, a door, a kettle, and let it be your bell: when it sounds, stop and take one breath. Day ten.

11.title: impermanence
11.hook: impermanence; the leaf, the mood, the year
11.howItsDone: Buddhists reflect on anicca in meditation by watching breath, sensations and thoughts arise and pass, and in daily life by recalling that all conditioned things change; some traditions use images like falling leaves, candles and sand mandalas swept away after completion.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the bell, a sound you follow down to silence. Your line was arrive. Did some ordinary sound become your bell? Day eleven.

Look at a leaf in October. Last spring it was a tight green bud. In summer it was so ordinary nobody noticed it. Now it's red and gold and loose on the branch, and next week it'll be on the sidewalk. Now look at your mood this morning, compared to right now. Different. Look at last year: the worry that kept you up in March, which you can barely remember. The leaf, the mood, the year. They're all doing the same thing, at different speeds. They're passing. The Buddha said that one fact, looked at closely, changes everything.

Anicca. In Pali, nicca means permanent, lasting, constant. Put an a in front and you get the opposite: not lasting. Impermanence. It's the first of what Buddhists call the three marks of existence, the three things true of everything that's made of parts and conditions. Anicca, impermanence. Dukkha, which you already know. And anatta, which is tomorrow. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, puts the first one in four words: "All created things perish." Now, that sounds obvious. Everyone knows things change. But here's the catch. We know it the way we know the sun is a star. True, and useless, because we don't live like it. We hold on to the good mood as if it'll stay. We treat the bad week as if it's forever. We're startled every single time something ends. So the Buddha didn't teach anicca as a fact to agree with. He taught it as something to see, again and again, in small things, until it sinks in. Watch a breath: it comes, and goes. Watch a thought: it arrives, and leaves. Watch a sound, like yesterday's bell, fade away. And here's the part that's easy to miss. Impermanence isn't only sad news. It's what makes change possible at all. If things were permanent, your grief would never soften. Your bad habit would never break. The seed would never grow. The same fact that takes the leaf in October brings the bud in April. This passes, both ways.
screen: `ANICCA — NOT LASTING.` · `THE FIRST OF THREE MARKS.` · `ALL CREATED THINGS PERISH.` · `WHY GRIEF CAN SOFTEN.` · then, large: `THIS PASSES.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about forty-five seconds. Watch something pass. Start with the breath: notice that each one begins, and ends, and is never quite the same as the last. Then notice sounds around you, arriving and leaving. If a feeling comes up, watch that too. You're not trying to hold anything or push anything away. Just watching things come and go, like leaves. The bell holds the time.
Anicca. Impermanence, the first of the three marks. Everything made of parts is passing, the hard things and the good ones. Eleventh word.
Your line: this passes. Today, when a strong feeling comes, good or bad, say it inside: this passes. Then watch to see if it's true. Day eleven.

trapdoor: what you thought: everything changes. obviously.

12.title: not-self
12.hook: not-self — who's actually in there? (the question, not the answer)
12.tomorrow: five, and they read like kindness
12.howItsDone: Buddhists explore anatta through meditation, observing body, feelings and thoughts without identifying with them, and through study; Theravada teaching centers on the five aggregates, while many Mahayana schools teach it through emptiness.

segments.voice: Yesterday: anicca, impermanence, the first mark. Your line was this passes. Did a strong feeling come, and did it? Day twelve.

Try this. Say the word I, and then try to point to it. Your finger goes to your chest, probably. But is that it? Your body has replaced most of its cells since you were a kid. Your opinions have changed. Your taste in music. Your memories are edited every time you remember them. Your mood changed twice before lunch. So who's the I that stayed the same through all of that? People have asked this for thousands of years. The Buddha asked it too, and his answer is famous and famously misunderstood. Today we're taking the question, not the answer.
screen: `SAY "I", THEN POINT TO IT.` → `CELLS, OPINIONS, MOODS, ALL CHANGING.` → `WHO'S ACTUALLY IN THERE?`

segments.voice: Anatta. Atta means self, the unchanging core, the owner. An-atta: not-self. It's the third mark of existence, after anicca and dukkha. Here's how the Buddha is remembered teaching it, in his second discourse, to the same five companions. He goes through what a person is made of. The texts count five heaps: the body, feelings, perceptions, mental formations, and consciousness. And he asks about each one. Is the body permanent or impermanent? Impermanent. Is what's impermanent something you can rest on, or does it wobble? It wobbles. Then is it right to say of it: this is mine, this is what I am, this is my self? No. And he goes through all five the same way. It's not a lecture. It's a series of questions. Look, and see. There's a moment in the discourses that fits today perfectly. A wanderer asks the Buddha straight out: is there a self? The Buddha is silent. Is there no self? Silent again. Later he explains to his attendant Ananda that either answer would have led the man into a wrong view. Anatta, many teachers say, is less a doctrine to believe than a way of looking: don't cling to anything as me or mine, and see what happens. Buddhist schools talk about this in different ways. Theravada teachers stress the five heaps and the practice of seeing them as not-self. Many Mahayana traditions speak of emptiness, and some of a Buddha-nature in every being. They share the practice of looking. Who's in there? Keep the question open.
screen: `ANATTA — NOT-SELF.` · `FIVE HEAPS, EACH ONE QUESTIONED.` · `IS THERE A SELF? SILENCE.` · `A WAY OF LOOKING, NOT A DOCTRINE.` · then, large: `WHO'S IN THERE?`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about forty-five seconds. Sit, and look. Notice a sensation: is it you, or something happening? Notice a thought passing: did you choose it, or did it just arrive? Notice a feeling. Don't answer the question. Don't decide anything. Just keep looking, gently, at whatever shows up, and let the question stay open. The bell holds the time.
Anatta. Not-self, the third mark: nothing in the five heaps can be held as me, mine, or my self. A question to keep looking into. Twelfth word.
Your line: look. Today, when you catch yourself saying I'm always like this, stop, and look: is it always? Is it you, or a mood passing through? Day twelve.

screen: `DAY 12 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: FIVE, AND THEY READ LIKE KINDNESS.`

13.title: five, and they read like kindness
13.hook: five, and they read like kindness
13.howItsDone: Lay Buddhists often recite the five precepts in Pali after taking refuge in the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha, at temple services, festivals and at home; some keep eight precepts on observance days.

segments.voice: Yesterday: anatta, not-self, a question kept open. Your line was look. Did you catch an I'm always like this, and look again? Day thirteen.

When people hear a religion has rules, they brace. They picture a long list of thou-shalt-nots, somebody stern at the top, and a lot of guilt. Buddhism has a short list too. Five lines. Millions of people say them, often every week, sometimes every day, standing in a temple in Sri Lanka or kneeling in a living room in Los Angeles. But when you actually read them, they don't sound like a list of rules. They sound like a promise to be easy to live next to. Today, the five.
screen: `A RELIGION HAS RULES.` → `FIVE LINES, SAID EVERY WEEK.` → `EASY TO LIVE NEXT TO.`

segments.voice: The precepts. In Pali, sila: conduct, virtue, the way you live. There are five for lay Buddhists. Not to kill or harm living beings. Not to take what isn't given. Not to cause harm through sex. Not to speak falsely. And not to take intoxicants that cloud the mind. That's the list. Now listen to how they're actually said. Each one is phrased the same way: I undertake the training rule to refrain from harming living beings. I undertake the training rule to refrain from taking what is not given. And so on. Notice the words. I undertake. Nobody is ordering anyone. You take them on yourself. And training rule. Not a law, not a commandment. Something you practice, fail at sometimes, and pick up again, the way you'd train for a race. There's a lovely teaching in the discourses that turns the whole thing around. It calls the five precepts five great gifts. When you keep them, the Buddha says, you give freedom from fear to countless beings. Everyone near you can relax. They don't have to worry you'll hurt them, rob them, betray them, lie to them, or lose control. And because you give them safety, you get to share in that safety too. That's why they read like kindness. They aren't about keeping yourself pure. They're about everyone else being able to breathe around you. Buddhists hold them in different ways. Some take all five for life. Some take them fresh on holy days. Monks and nuns take many more. But almost everyone begins with these five.
screen: `SILA — HOW YOU LIVE.` · `FIVE LINES FOR LAY BUDDHISTS.` · `I UNDERTAKE THE TRAINING RULE.` · `FIVE GREAT GIFTS: NO FEAR.` · then, large: `EASY TO LIVE NEXT TO.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about forty-five seconds. Think about the five: not harming, not taking, not betraying, not lying, not clouding the mind. Don't grade yourself. Just ask which one would make the biggest difference to the people around you this week. Pick that one. Picture someone near you feeling a little safer because of it. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
The precepts. Five training rules, taken on freely, that give everyone around you freedom from fear. Thirteenth word.
Your line: do less harm. Today, choose the precept you picked and keep it all day, one small act at a time, even if nobody notices. Day thirteen.

14.title: generosity
14.hook: generosity — the first practice taught to beginners, not the last
14.howItsDone: Buddhists practice dana by offering food, robes and medicine to monastics, most visibly on the morning alms round in Theravada countries, and by giving to others in daily life; many temples run entirely on donations, and some meditation teachers teach freely on a dana basis.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the precepts, five training rules that give others freedom from fear. Your line was do less harm. Which one did you keep? Day fourteen.

Two weeks. Look back at this one. The fourth truth, the path. Sati, remembering to notice. The bell. Anicca, this passes. Anatta, who's in there. The precepts. That's deep water for week two. So you might expect the next word to be even deeper, some advanced meditation. It isn't. It's the thing the Buddha usually taught first, to people who had never heard him before. Before the four truths. Before meditation. Picture a monk at dawn, barefoot, holding an empty bowl, walking past houses. Someone steps out with rice. Today, the first practice.
screen: `TWO WEEKS ON YOUR STRAND.` → `AN EMPTY BOWL AT DAWN.` → `THE PRACTICE THAT COMES FIRST.`

segments.voice: Dana. Giving. Generosity. When the Buddha taught people who were new to his teaching, the discourses say he often followed an order, a gradual talk. He started with giving. Then conduct. Then the good results those bring. Only when someone's heart was ready did he teach the four truths. Giving came first. Not because it's easy, but because it loosens the grip. You can't give with a closed hand. There's a line in the discourses, which Buddhists love, that goes roughly like this: if people knew, as I know, the fruit of giving and sharing, they wouldn't eat without giving, and they wouldn't let stinginess take root. Even their last bite, they'd share, if there were someone to share it with. And the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's old translation, says: "Let a man overcome anger by love, let him overcome evil by good; let him overcome the greedy by liberality, the liar by truth!" Liberality. Generosity. The answer to greed isn't a lecture. It's a gift. You can still see dana every morning in Thailand, Laos, Myanmar and Sri Lanka. Monks walk with their bowls, and people give food. Here's what surprises people: in the Theravada tradition, monks don't ask, and they don't store food for tomorrow. They depend on the giving. And the one who gives is usually understood to receive something too: merit, joy, a lighter heart. In both Theravada and Mahayana lists of the perfections a buddha develops, generosity stands first. Not the last step. The first one.
